name: The Tourbillon Vestige

detectability.signature: Gravitational microlensing arcs smeared across background stars with faint weakly-interacting particle traces

proximity: Instruments register unusual gravitational readings despite no visible mass
Starlight behind the region smears into slow arcs
contact: Ships feel a tidal kneading along their keels crossing the halo
Every sensor reading arrives doubled and slightly delayed
prolonged_exposure: Chronic instrument drift forces constant recalibration
Gradual orbital decay toward the concentration's dense heart

phenomena: Light bending around the invisible mass
Gravitational lensing of background stars into twin images
Exotic particles detectable on sensors in trace quantities
opportunities: Unique research opportunity into dark matter physics
Hidden base location screened from distant observation
known_incidents: The cartographers' guild charted the Vestige only after losing four probe strings to its lensing maze
description: Nothing is visibly there, and that is precisely the problem: 2.7 astronomical units of warped starlight where no light source exists. Background constellations bend into matched pairs as they pass behind the halo, tracing the outline of a mass that refuses every form of direct observation. Pilots describe the region as navigating inside a watch case with the movement removed.

The concentration behaves with metronomic patience, wheeling through its long galactic orbit and dragging navigation charts out of date once per millennium. Gravitational gradients within the halo are gentle but relentless, and ships that loiter find themselves spiraling toward a core they can measure but never see. Instruments double-report everything, as if reality here were keeping two ledgers.

Deep survey teams identified the Vestige as the collapsed remnant of a dark filament, two billion years of accretion compressed into a lens. Its discovery rewrote local mass maps and embarrassed three governments whose borders had been drawn straight through it. The cartographers' guild still posts a standing bounty for probe strings recovered from its foci.

Smugglers prize the halo because nothing distant can see into it, while researchers prize it because nothing within it can hide from gravimetry. Traffic advisories recommend transiting perpendicular to the long axis and trusting mass detectors over eyes. The Vestige asks only one thing of visitors: bring your own light.
